items.prose: An interviewer keeps extending one question. Use the round figures: L3 20 ns, DRAM 100 ns, NVMe 100 µs, London to New York 60 ms.
items.question: Four follow-ups on the latency ladder.

parts.question: How many L3 reads take as long as one NVMe read?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put both in nanoseconds.

byKey.dram: 1,000 is the count of DRAM reads. An L3 read takes 20 ns, not 100.
byKey.l1: 100,000 uses 1 ns, the L1 time. An L3 read takes 20 ns.

parts.question: How many main-memory reads take as long as one London to New York round trip?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. 60 ms is 60,000,000 ns.

parts.question: A handler makes 3 main-memory reads a message, and one NVMe read per 1,000 messages. What is the average cost a message, in ns?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Share the NVMe read over 1,000 messages.

byKey.nvme: The NVMe read happens once per 1,000 messages, not every message.
byKey.dram: Add the NVMe share: 100 ns a message.

explain.text: $3 \times 100 = 300$ ns from memory, plus $100{,}000 / 1{,}000 = 100$ ns from the drive: 400 ns.

parts.question: As a fraction, what is the NVMe share of that cost compared with the DRAM share?

options.why: You divided the DRAM share by the NVMe share.
You compared one read with one read, not the shares per message.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 100 ns with 300 ns.

explain.text: The rare slow read adds 100 ns a message; the three fast reads add 300 ns. A rare slow access can still cost as much as the common ones.

items.title: A cache simulator
items.prose: Turn this level's hand counts into code. A cache has `num_lines` lines of 64 bytes, in sets of `ways` lines. Byte address `a` is in line `a / 64`, which lives in set `(a / 64) % (num_lines / ways)`. A full set drops its least recently used line.
items.question: Write `count_misses`: start empty and return the number of misses.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Ten hidden tests. They include the l2 clash, an 8 × 8 matrix both ways and strides 2 and 3. Also an empty list and a set one line too small.

feedback.correct: That's it. Find the set, look for the line, and keep the set in recency order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test and trace it by hand.

explain.text: Keep each set as a list with the most recent line at the front. A hit moves its line to the front. A miss puts the new line there, and a full set drops its back line, the least recently used.

items.title: From a[i] to a register
items.prompt: Say aloud, in two minutes, what happens from `a[i]` in your code to the value arriving in a register. Time yourself, and use this level's round figures. Then open the model answer and tick the rubric.
items.model:
**1. The address is virtual.** `a[i]` becomes the address of `a` plus `8 * i` for a double. That address is virtual: a page number and a 12-bit offset into a 4 KiB page.

**2. Translation.** The core looks the page up in the TLB. A hit costs almost nothing. A miss walks the four-level page table: up to four memory reads, about 400 ns if none is cached.

**3. Cache lines.** The L1 lookup starts from the virtual address while the TLB translates, and the physical tag confirms the hit. The core wants the 64-byte line that holds the address. Eight doubles share a line, so a loop in order misses once per eight reads.

**4. The levels.** L1 answers in about 1 ns, L2 in about 4 ns and L3 in about 20 ns. If all three miss, main memory answers in about 100 ns. The line is copied in, evicting the least recently used line of its set.

**5. The slow cases.** If the page has no frame yet, the access faults. A minor fault costs about 1 µs. One that reads from an SSD costs about 100 µs, and from a spinning disk about 10 ms.

**6. Why it matters.** The same `a[i]` can cost 1 ns or 100 µs: five powers of ten. So layout and access order decide speed: keep hot data small, contiguous and in the order you walk it.

rubric.text: Says the address is virtual and is translated to a physical one through the page table
Names the TLB: a hit is nearly free, a miss walks up to four levels, about 400 ns
Says memory moves in 64-byte lines, so neighbouring data arrives together
Gives L1, L2, L3 and DRAM with round figures of 1, 4, 20 and 100 ns
Mentions a page fault or a miss to disk, with its cost
Closes with why layout and access order matter

items.prose: A 1,200 × 1,200 matrix of doubles is stored row by row. The L1 cache is 32 KiB: 512 lines in 64 sets of 8 ways. Count only L1 misses, at 100 ns each.
items.question: Five follow-ups on loop order.

parts.question: How many misses does the row-by-row sum make?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line serves 8 reads.

byKey.all: Row by row, 7 of every 8 reads hit.
byKey.rows: 1,200 is the number of rows. Each row spans 150 lines.

explain.text: 1.44 million doubles at 8 a line is 180,000 lines, each missed once.

parts.question: How many misses does the column-by-column sum make?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Can a line survive until the walk returns to it?

byKey.rows: That is the row order. A column touches 1,200 lines, more than the cache holds.

explain.text: One column touches 1,200 different lines, and the cache holds 512. By the time the walk returns, each line is gone.

parts.question: At 100 ns a miss, how long does the row order take, in ms?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply misses by 100 ns.

parts.question: And the column order, in ms?

feedback.correct: 144 ms, eight times the row order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply 1.44 million misses by 100 ns.

byKey.sec: 0.144 is in seconds. The question asks for ms.

explain.text: $1.44 \times 10^6 \times 100$ ns is 144 ms, eight times the row order.

parts.question: For a 32 × 64 matrix, how many misses does the column order make?

widget.accept: 256: the matrix fits, so each line misses once.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does a 32 × 64 matrix fit in 32 KiB?

byKey.all: 2,048 would need lines to leave. 32 KiB holds the whole 16 KiB matrix.

explain.text: 32 × 64 × 8 bytes is 16 KiB: 256 lines, 4 in each of 64 sets, under 8 ways. Nothing is evicted, so both orders miss 256 times.

items.question: Fill in every offset and both sizes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r1c1: `b` is 8 bytes, so it waits for offset 8.
byKey.r3c1: `c` ends at 17, and `d` needs a multiple of 2: 18.
byKey.r4c1: `d` ends at 20, which rounds up to a multiple of 8: 24.
byKey.r4c3: `c` ends at 12, which rounds up to a multiple of 8: 16.

explain.text: Declared, `a` wastes 7 bytes before `b` and the tail wastes 4: 24 bytes. Sorted, the small fields pack after `b` and only the tail pads: 16 bytes. A third smaller, from moving two fields.

items.prose: A handler reads a 256 MiB table at random. Each read costs 100 ns. On a TLB miss it also pays a 30 ns walk; take that as given. The walk is partly cached, so it is far below a full 400 ns walk. The TLB holds 64 entries.
items.question: Four follow-ups on page size.

parts.question: With 4 KiB pages, what is the TLB hit rate?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the pages in 256 MiB first.

byKey.small: 0.39% is a 64 MiB table. This one is four times bigger.

parts.question: What is the average cost of a read, in ns?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the walk, weighted by the miss rate.

byKey.walk: 130 charges every read the walk. 0.098% of reads hit.

explain.text: $100 + (1 - 64 / 65{,}536) \times 30 = 129.97$ ns. Almost every read pays the walk.

parts.question: With 2 MiB pages, what is the average cost of a read, in ns?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. 256 MiB is 128 huge pages.

byKey.all: 64 entries hold only half of the 128 huge pages.
byKey.none: Half the pages are in the TLB now.

explain.text: 256 MiB is 128 pages of 2 MiB; 64 fit, so the hit rate is 50%. The cost is $100 + 0.5 \times 30 = 115$ ns.

parts.question: How much faster is that than with 4 KiB pages, as a percentage of the 4 KiB cost?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the saving by the 4 KiB cost.

byKey.walk: 15% is the 15 ns walk saving over a 100 ns read. Divide by 129.97.
byKey.other: 13% divides by the new cost, 115. Divide by the old one.

explain.text: The saving is $129.97 - 115 = 14.97$ ns, and $14.97 / 129.97 \approx 11.5\%$. Changing the page size changed no code.

items.prose: A handler branches on `if (type == 'A')`. Types arrive in random order: 80% adds, 10% cancels, 10% trades. Each message has a 5 µs budget, and a wrong guess costs 5 ns.
items.question: Should you rewrite the branch branchless?

options.text: No: it costs about 1 ns of 5,000 ns, 0.02%. Measure first.
Yes: branches on random data are always worth removing
options.why: Only if they matter. 1 ns is 0.02% of the budget.

options.text: Yes: it is wrong half the time
options.why: The best guess, 'add', is wrong 20% of the time, not half.
A wrong guess costs about 5 ns. Here it is wrong 20% of the time.

feedback.correct: No. The branch is not where the time goes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out its cost first.

byKey.c: Guessing 'add' every time is right 80% of the time.

explain.text: Wrong 20% of the time at 5 ns is 1 ns a message: 0.02% of 5 µs. A rewrite would risk bugs for nothing. Measure where the time goes before you optimise.

items.title: A branch in a hot loop, aloud
items.question: Start the clock and answer aloud. Then mark your answer against the model.

widget.prompt:
A hot loop copies every price at or below a limit into an output array:

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
    if (p[i] <= limit) out[k++] = p[i];
```

One pass covers 10,000,000 prices. About 30% pass the limit, in random order. The rest of the loop costs about 1 ns a price, and a wrong guess costs 5 ns.

An interviewer asks three things. How does the branch predictor treat this branch, and what does it cost on one pass? How would you write the loop with no branch? When would that rewrite not help? Answer aloud in two minutes.
followUps: Half the prices pass, still in random order. What does the branch cost on one pass now?
A compiler turns `if (x <= limit) sum += x;` into a conditional move by itself. Why does it leave this loop's branch alone?
How would you show that the rewrite helped?
widget.model:
**The predictor.** The core reaches the `if` before the comparison is done, so it guesses the outcome and runs ahead. The guess comes from the branch's recent history, as with a two-bit counter. When the guess is wrong, the work done past the branch is thrown away, which costs about 5 ns.

**The cost here.** The order is random, so the history says nothing about the next price. Guessing "keep" is wrong 70% of the time and guessing "skip" 30%, so no predictor beats 30% wrong. That is $10{,}000{,}000 \times 0.3 = 3{,}000{,}000$ wrong guesses, and $3{,}000{,}000 \times 5$ ns $= 15$ ms. The rest of the loop costs $10{,}000{,}000 \times 1$ ns $= 10$ ms. So the branch is 15 of 25 ms, 60% of the pass. A two-bit counter does a little worse, because a run of passes tips it to "keep": on this data it is wrong about 36% of the time, about 18 ms.

**The rewrite.** Store every price, and move the write position on only when the price passes:

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    out[k] = p[i];           // always store
    k += (p[i] <= limit);    // the comparison is 1 or 0
}
```

The comparison becomes a number added to `k`, not a jump, so there is nothing to guess. A price that fails is overwritten by the next one. So `out` needs room for all `n` prices, not only the kept ones. If the body stays near 1 ns, the pass takes about 10 ms instead of 25 ms: 2.5 times faster.

**When it does not help.** When the data are predictable, the branch is nearly free. If 99% pass, guessing "keep" is wrong 1% of the time: $10{,}000{,}000 \times 0.01 \times 5$ ns $= 0.5$ ms. Sorted prices fool the predictor about once, where they cross the limit. Then the store on every price costs more than the branch did, so measure both loops on real prices before choosing.

**The follow-ups.** (1) Half pass: $10{,}000{,}000 \times 0.5 \times 5$ ns $= 25$ ms, the worst case for random data. (2) In a running sum the add can be done every time and the result picked without a jump, so the compiler emits a conditional move. Here the store happens only for some prices. A compiler may not add a store the code does not make: `out` may end where the kept prices end, so the extra store could land past it. (3) Time both loops many times on the same recorded prices and compare the spread, not one run. A tool such as `perf stat` also counts the branch misses directly.

rubric.text: Tick only if all are given: the predictor guesses before the comparison is done, from the branch's history, and a wrong guess throws away the work past it, about 5 ns. On random data no guess beats 30% wrong
The cost: 3,000,000 wrong guesses at 5 ns is 15 ms, against 10 ms for the rest of the loop
Tick only if both are given: the rewrite stores every price and adds the comparison, 1 or 0, to `k`, so there is no jump. Says `out` needs room for all `n` prices
Tick only if both are given: when it does not help, predictable data such as sorted prices or 99% passing (0.5 ms) make the branch nearly free. Says to measure both loops

feedback.correct: Compare what you said with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Compare what you said with the model and tick the rubric.

explain.text: On random data the branch is wrong at least 30% of the time: 15 ms of misses against 10 ms of work. Storing every price and adding the comparison to `k` leaves nothing to guess. On predictable data the branch is nearly free, so measure first.
